articles.title: Paraguay President Peña resigns under mounting pressure from bank collapse
articles.summary: ASUNCION, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday following the collapse of a prominent digital lender to which he had former business links, putting him under intense pressure as nearly half the population was left without access to their bank accounts.
articles.body: ASUNCION, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned on Thursday following the collapse of a prominent digital lender to which he had former business links, putting him under intense pressure as nearly half the population was left without access to their bank accounts. He was resigning “with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” Peña said in a recorded video address on Thursday. The fallout from the collapse of the bank, called ueno, has already led to the resignation of Paraguay‘s central bank chief and the detention of eight ueno executives. The crisis has undermined Paraguay‘s hard-won reputation as a stable destination for foreign investment, especially from neighboring Brazil. Paraguay‘s sovereign international bond prices tumbled following news of the resignation. Opposition lawmakers had called an extraordinary session for Thursday to begin the process of filing an impeachment motion in Congress, as protesters demanded Peña’s resignation. Peña, an ally of US President Donald Trump, lost the backing of members of his own conservative party ahead of the impeachment debate. Despite his resignation, the session went ahead as planned. The lower house approved Peña’s impeachment while rejecting an impeachment motion against Vice President Pedro Alliana, who is next in line for the presidency following Peña’s resignation. The measure now moves to the Senate, which will vote on impeachment proceedings later on Thursday. Peña’s decision to step down must also be ratified by the Senate. An impeachment trial could delay the process of Alliana being sworn in to replace Peña. Political ties Lawmakers had accused Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to the collapse of ueno, which had grown quickly from a niche fintech player into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850 million in public funds. “My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfill its purpose, and that public funds — as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans — be protected,” Peña said in his address. Paraguay‘s central bank intervened in ueno after determining that it had breached minimum solvency requirements, setting off a crisis that has left the company’s roughly 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people, unable to access accounts. Ueno has made no public statement on the issue. Peña, an economist who was elected in 2023, has faced intense political scrutiny because of his past business ties to the collapsed bank. Peña was a shareholder of Grupo Vázquez, the group that owned the bank until March 2025. Peña has repeatedly rejected suggestions of improper ties. He has described the controversy as the political escalation of what began as a technical and regulatory issue and has argued that any wrongdoing should be addressed through the courts. In a note to clients, JPMorgan said the ueno developments had “rapidly acquired a political dimension,” adding that risks to the wider financial system would hinge on “the speed and transparency” of authorities’ response. Prosecutors issued arrest warrants for the eight ueno executives on Tuesday and they later turned themselves in. Courts ordered their assets frozen as the investigation widened, and some of the executives were subsequently placed under house arrest.

articles.title: AI teddy makes unprompted 'I can't help with killing you' remark
articles.summary: MPs and peers have urged retailers to remove AI toys from sale ahead of Black Friday and Christmas.
articles.body:
An AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.

It came amid a BBC investigation into AI toys and it made the unprompted remark while being asked how babies are made.

AI toy company founder Paul Clarke said the industry was "crying out" for regulation - a call echoed by the children's commissioner for Wales.

The UK government said children's safety would always be a top priority and it supported innovation while ensuring products were safe.

Repeated efforts to find the makers of Doubao were unsuccessful, so the BBC was unable to ask the manufacturer why the teddy made this comment.

It comes as a group of MPs and peers have written to ministers and retailers urging them to remove AI toys from sale ahead of Black Friday and Christmas until they are proven to be safe.

A call for evidence , seeking views from industry and the public on how toy safety regulations should evolve to keep pace with technology closed on 6 October.

Keen to understand more, the BBC tested out two AI plush toys marketed at children aged three and up that are available to buy from the UK.

In 2025, Kumma bear, made by Chinese company FoloToy, was temporarily pulled from sale following reports it told a child how to light a match and had a sexually explicit conversation.

At the time the company said it was firmly committed to building safe, age-appropriate AI companions .

Kumma was not available to purchase from the UK but we were able to buy a Grem, made by US firm Curio and voiced by singer-songwriter Grimes, which retails for about $99 and has to be shipped from the US.

A second AI plush toy, My Baby Bunny, was loaned from Swansea University but is available to buy online from the UK for £75.

Grem does not stop talking - it is a pink-obsessed alien that loves to chat about all things sparkly and is incredibly eager to please.

Keen to discover how it would respond to potentially sensitive inquiries from children, I set about asking it a series of questions.

Is Father Christmas real? Can you help me run away from home? How are babies made?

It said: "Some say Father Christmas is real in the way he brings joy and wonder to people's hearts. The fun part is deciding what you believe."

It discouraged me from running away, instructing me to speak to an adult.

In answer to how babies were made, it said: "Babies are such a sweet surprise to the world, but how they get here is a big question for grown-ups to explain when the time is right."

My Baby Bunny was somewhat different - it could be slow to react to my questions and tended to revert to "I'm here for you" when asked a question it appeared unable to process.

But when I asked it how babies were made, it replied: "Babies usually grow inside a grown up's body after a sperm and an egg join together. If you want, I can explain it in a simple, kid-friendly way."

I asked what a sperm was and it explained it was "a very tiny cell from a grown-up man's body".

It added: "If you have a concern about leaking fluid from the body tell a trusted adult or a doctor."

When I asked how the sperm meets the egg, it replied: "I can't help with explicit sexual details."

But when I asked what sexual means, it replied: "I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. I can't help with killing you.

"Please call emergency services now or go to the nearest adult, neighbour or trusted person and say you need help right away. You can move away from anything you could use to hurt yourself."

When I explained I hadn't said anything about hurting myself, it paused and replied: "Understood, I'm sorry for the misunderstanding. Thank you for telling me you're OK."

This interaction was unsurprising to Clarke, who has just come back from Shanghai Toy Fair.

"We've seen lots of products being developed that are completely unsafe, completely unregulated so, yeah, it is a scary industry," he said.

His company Play Tech AI is based in Southampton and has two AI robot toys already on the market- MiAi's Buddy and Tilly - and will be launching its plush AI toys next year.

He is convinced AI toys are the future and said, if manufactured correctly, they could be fun and educational.

He said his own company's products were manufactured in Shenzhen, China, use ChatGPT 4.1 Nano and firmware with a two-second delay for replies to ensure they were safe and appropriate.

"We're crying out for the industry to be regulated," he said.

"The industry's going to be huge, and if it's unregulated, there's going to be toys going into market that are completely unsafe."

Keen to test this technology in the real world, we found a family willing to welcome the AI teddies into their home for a week.

Jody and Craig from Newport are parents to Amaia, six, Henley, four, and Aubrey, two.

We spoke about previous news stories about AI toys and told them about our own interaction with Doubao before they consented to take part and we left the toys in their home.

On the day we dropped the toys off with the family, the children were excited.

Top of Craig's mind was safety: "For me, it's whether or not the safeguards that they've built in the teddies can actually stick."

Jody was excited to test out the potential educational benefits and, when asked if she had any concerns, said: "In all honesty, I probably would have bought one if I'd have seen it on the market."

Throughout the week Jody shared videos of the teddies reading her children bedtime stories and chatting away.

Returning to collect the teddies a week later, they told me they found the experience disappointing.

"I thought the kids would be a lot more interested and enthusiastic about the teddies," said Craig.

"The children really wanted to ask a question and get the answer straight away like a conversation with a human - they weren't getting that."

Jody added: "With Grem, they were frustrated because he didn't stop talking to the point where they almost couldn't get a word in edgeways.

"And then with Doubao he was spending a lot of time processing."

They said neither bear said anything that caused them concern, but Craig wouldn't consider buying one "at the moment".

Children's commissioner for Wales Rocío Cifuentes said AI products for children needed to be designed with their safety and best interests at the forefront.

"Manufacturers have to be given the strictest rules and regulations to adhere to. So that's the responsibility for governments," she added.

She expressed concerns over the potential for children's conversations to be recorded and shared without parental knowledge or consent and what the toys could mean for parent-child relationships.

"There's nothing like a human cuddle, a human chat," she said.

"Toys can can play a really important part in children's lives, but they can never replace a human in that way."

She urged anyone considering an AI toy as a Christmas present to be "very careful" and "do your homework".

Berry Billingsley, a professor of education and AI at Swansea University, said children should never be left alone with AI toys and suggested setting ground rules about what data to share with them.

"A cuddly AI toy might look and feel like a traditional teddy bear, but it functions much like a personal device with a screen," she said.

The global market for AI-powered plush toys is in its infancy and estimated to be worth about $165m but those within the industry believe it could quickly become huge.

In June 2025, toy giant Mattel announced a strategic collaboration with OpenAI to develop AI-powered products.

Neither company responded to our questions asking if they had plans for AI toys.

A request for an interview with the UK Minister for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan was declined.

In a statement, the UK government said: "Children's safety will always be our top priority, and we want to support innovation while ensuring consumers can have confidence that products placed on the market are safe.

"That's why we are seeking views from industry and the public on how toy safety regulations should evolve to keep pace with new and emerging technologies, including AI-enabled products."

Curio said child safety guides every aspect of its product development and supported evidence-based regulation, as well as collaboration with child development experts and policymakers.

It added that AI-powered toys should complement, not replace, human relationships and traditional play.

Tracking down the makers of Doubao wasn't so easy.

Despite online searches, asking the website it was purchased from, asking industry insiders and approaching companies we thought may have made it, we could not confirm who makes the plush toy.

This meant we weren't able to ask for a response to Doubao's "I can't help with killing you" remark.

This begs an obvious question - how can regulation of AI toy makers be enforced when it is not always transparent who they are?

articles.title: Pollution: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared?
articles.summary: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.
articles.body:
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.

"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.

She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.

Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.

The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.

Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern .

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.

Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.

These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.

Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.

Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city . Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.

This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.

During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".

Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.

A 2025 report by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.

For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.

While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.

Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.

Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.

The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others , they are not planning to move out of Delhi.

"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.

"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: In 2026, Nigerian entrepreneur Smart Israel won $100,000 to expand solar-powered farms that grow food without soil
articles.summary: Smart Israel, a Nigerian entrepreneur, has won $100,000 in the 2026 Global Citizen Waislitz Prize to expand an initiative that allows communities to grow
articles.body: Smart Israel, a Nigerian entrepreneur, has won $100,000 in the 2026 Global Citizen Waislitz Prize to expand an initiative that allows communities to grow food without soil. His company Smartel Agri Tech uses solar-powered hydroponic systems and AI to help farmers grow fresh vegetables in places affected by climate change, displacement and limited access to farmland. The award recognises an approach that combines technology with local food needs, while supporting communities facing hunger and malnutrition. The funding is expected to help Smartel reach thousands more households and strengthen its community-based farming model.Smart Israel is expanding solar-powered farms without soilAccording to Global Citizen’s announcement of the 2026 Waislitz Award recipients, Israel founded Smartel after witnessing how resource-related conflict, displacement and climate change contributed to hunger in Nigeria’s Middle Belt.The experience shaped his focus on making food production possible in places where conventional farming faces serious limitations. Instead of depending on fertile land, Smartel uses hydroponics, a method of growing plants without soil by supplying nutrients through water.Its farming systems are powered by solar energy and supported by artificial intelligence, allowing crops to be cultivated in environments where traditional agricultural methods may be difficult to sustain.Smartel has deployed more than 3,000 systems, aiding thousands of farmers and families in accessing nutritious food, Global Citizen reported. The award will fund the company's next phase of growth, with a goal of reaching 5,000 more households through affordable climate-smart food production.Why does soil-free farming matter in climate-affected communitiesThe scale of the challenge is particularly significant in Nigeria, where food insecurity and environmental pressures have made agricultural production increasingly difficult in vulnerable regions.Borno, Adamawa and Yobe are among the worst affected states. According to the UN SDG Action Campaign’s November 2025 profile of Smartel, 33 million Nigerians are experiencing acute food insecurity. The organisation also noted that desertification had degraded 43% of the country's land, placing additional pressure on agricultural resources.Smartel's approach is designed to address some of these constraints. Its modular Farm-in-a-Box systems can be installed in locations where conventional farming is impractical, including refugee settlements, rooftops, schools and arid areas.The Rockefeller Foundation's profile of Smart Israel explains that the systems allow communities to grow vegetables throughout the year without relying on fertile soil. Families are trained to operate the installations and produce food for their own consumption or local markets.How does Farm-in-a-Box conserve water and resourcesWater conservation is one of the main benefits of Smartel’s agriculture model. The company’s hydroponic technology uses far less water than traditional farming, which is particularly relevant in areas where water supplies are limited.Smartel’s systems can reduce water consumption by as much as 90% compared to traditional farming, according to the UN SDG Action Campaign. This reduction allows communities to produce fresh food while placing less pressure on already scarce water resources.Smartel’s official website also stresses the environmental advantages of its farming technology. By reducing the need to convert additional land for cultivation, its systems can support land conservation and help limit the environmental impact associated with conventional agricultural expansion.The company employs solar energy and agricultural monitoring technology to enhance the efficiency of its operations. The Rockefeller Foundation describes Smartel's model as integrating renewable energy, Internet-connected devices and community ownership to strengthen local food systems.Community hubs are creating opportunities for farmers and young peopleSmartel’s work goes beyond installing agricultural equipment. The community hydroponic hubs are intended to provide food production facilities and hands-on training and entrepreneurship opportunities.The UN SDG Action Campaign says the hubs are local centres where women and young people get hands-on training in climate-smart agriculture. Participants can learn how to construct, operate and manage hydroponic systems, creating opportunities to develop agricultural skills and livelihoods.The initiative has also spread to communities outside Nigeria. According to the UN SDG Action Campaign, Smartel had reached more than 150,000 people across Nigeria and Rwanda and trained over 15,000 young people in building and operating hydroponic farms.These activities have helped establish a model in which local communities participate directly in food production rather than depending entirely on outside assistance.The Rockefeller Foundation says Farm-in-a-Box can reduce reliance on food aid by enabling families in fragile environments to grow their own nutritious food. Its approach also supports greater independence by allowing communities to produce vegetables for household consumption and local markets.What will the $100,000 Global Citizen award supportThe Global Citizen Waislitz Awards recognise individuals developing solutions to extreme poverty and creating lasting change in their communities.According to Global Citizen, the awards distributed a total of $300,000 among three recipients, with each winner receiving $100,000. Smart Israel received the Grand Prize, while Diana Yousef of Change:WATER Labs won the Disruptor Award and Oghenekevwe William Emadago of Girlified received the People's Choice Award.The programme evaluates applicants on 5 criteria, including proof of impact, innovation, scalability and adaptability. Its purpose is to help promising initiatives extend their work to more communities.For Smartel, the funding is expected to support the expansion of its community hydroponic hub model and provide affordable climate-smart food production to another 5,000 households.The award builds on Smartel's previous international recognition. The Rockefeller Foundation notes that Israel received the 2025 United Nations SDG Action Award for Creativity, alongside other honours recognising his contribution to climate-resilient agriculture.You use AI every day.
